cards.name: Solar Eclipse
cards.type_label: The Moon passing in front of the Sun
cards.summary: A solar eclipse happens when the Moon passes between the Sun and Earth and its shadow falls on Earth. Where the Moon covers only part of the Sun the eclipse is partial. Inside the narrow path of the Moon's dark umbra it is total, and the Sun's faint outer atmosphere, the corona, appears around the black lunar disk. When the Moon is near its farthest from Earth it looks too small to cover the Sun, leaving a bright ring in an annular eclipse. Solar eclipses happen only at new Moon, and somewhere on Earth sees between two and five of them every year.
cards.fact: The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon but also about 400 times farther away, so the two look almost exactly the same size in our sky.

cards.name: Lunar Eclipse
cards.type_label: The Moon passing through Earth's shadow
cards.summary: A lunar eclipse happens when Earth passes between the Sun and the Moon and Earth's shadow falls across the full Moon. In a penumbral eclipse the Moon only dims slightly; in a partial eclipse part of it enters Earth's dark umbra; in a total eclipse all of it does. Sunlight bent through Earth's atmosphere still reaches the Moon during totality and turns it copper red, lit by all the world's sunrises and sunsets at once. Unlike a solar eclipse, a lunar eclipse can be seen from the whole night side of Earth and is safe to watch without any filter.
cards.fact: Earth's shadow at the Moon's distance is nearly three times as wide as the Moon, so totality can last for more than an hour and a half.

cards.name: Comets
cards.type_label: Icy small bodies of the Solar System
cards.summary: Comets are icy bodies left over from the formation of the Solar System, from a few hundred metres to tens of kilometres across. Most spend their lives far beyond the planets. When one swings in towards the Sun its ices turn to gas and release dust, forming a bright head, the coma, and tails that can stretch for millions of kilometres: a curved, whitish dust tail and a straight, blue ion tail blown directly away from the Sun by the solar wind. Each of your comets is listed below by its designation; select one to read about its orbit.
cards.fact: A comet's tails always point away from the Sun, so a comet heading back out of the inner Solar System travels tail-first.
